q: A colourless salt solution X gives a white precipitate with a little NaOH solution that dissolves in excess NaOH. With aqueous ammonia it gives a white precipitate that also dissolves in excess. Passing H2S into its ammoniacal solution gives a white precipitate. Which cation is present?
why: Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric and also forms soluble [Zn(NH3)4]^2+ in excess ammonia, and ZnS is white. Al(OH)3 dissolves in excess NaOH but not in excess ammonia. Pb(OH)2 is not dissolved by ammonia and PbS is black, while Mg(OH)2 does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

q: In an iodometric estimation, copper(II) ions react with excess iodide to liberate iodine (2Cu2+ + 4I- -> 2CuI + I2), and the iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulfate (I2 + 2S2O3^2- -> 2I- + S4O6^2-). A 25.0 mL sample of the copper(II) solution needs 20.0 mL of 0.100 M thiosulfate. What is the molarity of Cu2+?
why: Each I2 consumes 2 thiosulfate and each I2 comes from 2 Cu2+, so Cu2+ : thiosulfate = 1 : 1. Moles = 0.100 x 0.0200 = 2.00 x 10^-3 mol in 25.0 mL, giving 0.0800 M. Using a 2:1 ratio gives 0.0400 M, which comes from forgetting the 2 Cu2+ per I2.

q: Among O2^2-, O2^-, O2^+ and O2, which one is paramagnetic and has a bond order of 2.5?
why: O2^+ has 11 valence electrons in the molecular orbital scheme, giving (8 - 3)/2 = 2.5 with one unpaired electron in pi*. O2^- has bond order 1.5 and O2 has 2, both paramagnetic but with different bond orders. O2^2- has bond order 1 and is diamagnetic.

q: One mole of PCl3 is completely hydrolysed by excess water. How many moles of NaOH are needed to neutralise all the acidic products completely? (Phosphorous acid is dibasic.)
why: PCl3 + 3H2O -> H3PO3 + 3HCl. H3PO3 has two P-OH groups (the third H is bonded to P and is not acidic), so it consumes 2 mol NaOH, and 3 HCl consume 3 mol, total 5 mol. Treating H3PO3 as tribasic gives the tempting 6 mol.

q: Phosphorous acid disproportionates on heating: 4H3PO3 -> 3H3PO4 + PH3. What mass of PH3 forms when 8.2 g of H3PO3 (molar mass 82 g/mol) is heated completely? (PH3 = 34 g/mol)
why: Moles of H3PO3 = 8.2/82 = 0.10 mol. Four moles give one mole of PH3, so PH3 = 0.025 mol, mass = 0.025 x 34 = 0.85 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 3.4 g and using a 3 : 1 ratio gives 1.13 g.

q: XeF6 reacts completely with water: XeF6 + 3H2O -> XeO3 + 6HF. How many moles of HF are formed from 24.5 g of XeF6? (Xe = 131, F = 19 g/mol)
why: Molar mass of XeF6 = 131 + 114 = 245 g/mol, so 24.5 g is 0.100 mol. Each mole gives 6 mol HF, so 0.600 mol HF forms. Using the 3 water molecules in place of 6 HF gives 0.30 mol.

q: In acidic solution, MnO4- is reduced to Mn2+. How many moles of MnO4- are needed to oxidise 1 mol of FeC2O4 completely to Fe3+ and CO2?
why: Fe2+ -> Fe3+ releases 1 e-, and C2O4^2- -> 2CO2 releases 2 e-, so 3 mol e- per mole of FeC2O4. MnO4- accepts 5 e-, so 3/5 = 0.6 mol. Counting only the iron (0.2) or only the oxalate (0.4) is the typical slip.

q: How many stereoisomers (counting each optical isomer separately) are possible for the complex ion [Co(en)2Cl2]^+, where en is ethane-1,2-diamine?
why: The trans isomer has a mirror plane and is achiral (1 isomer). The cis isomer lacks a mirror plane and exists as a pair of enantiomers (2 isomers). The total is 3; answering 2 counts cis and trans only.

q: Which pair of complexes has the same geometry but different magnetic behaviour?
why: [NiCl4]^2- (Ni2+, d8, weak-field Cl-) is tetrahedral with two unpaired electrons, while [Ni(CO)4] (Ni(0), d10) is tetrahedral and diamagnetic. [Ni(CN)4]^2- and [PdCl4]^2- are both square planar and diamagnetic, so they match in both properties. The other two pairs differ in geometry.

q: Lithium nitrate decomposes on heating as 4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2. What total volume of gases (at STP, 22.4 L/mol, NO2 treated as a gas) forms from 6.9 g of LiNO3 (69 g/mol)?
why: 6.9 g is 0.100 mol LiNO3. It gives 0.100 mol NO2 and 0.0250 mol O2, a total of 0.125 mol, which is 0.125 x 22.4 = 2.80 L. Forgetting the O2 gives 2.24 L, and using the sodium nitrate pattern gives only 1.12 L.

q: In the Hall-Heroult process a current of 1.00 x 10^4 A is passed for 9.65 hours through a cell producing aluminium at 100% current efficiency. What mass of Al is deposited? (F = 96500 C/mol, Al = 27 g/mol)
why: Charge = 1.00 x 10^4 x 9.65 x 3600 = 3.474 x 10^8 C, which is 3600 mol of electrons. Al3+ needs 3 e-, so moles of Al = 1200 and mass = 32.4 kg. Using 1 e- per Al gives 97.2 kg, while 2 e- gives 48.6 kg.

q: The brown ring complex [Fe(H2O)5(NO)]^2+ has a spin-only magnetic moment of about 3.87 BM. Treating the nitrosyl ligand as NO+, which description of the iron is correct?
why: The overall charge is +2 and water is neutral, so Fe + (+1 from NO+) = +2 gives Fe(+1), which is d7. Three unpaired electrons give sqrt(15) = 3.87 BM, matching the data. Fe(+2) would require NO as a neutral ligand and does not match the d7 count.
opts: Fe(+2), d6 with three unpaired electrons
Fe(+3), d5 with three unpaired electrons
Fe(+1), d7 with three unpaired electrons
Fe(+1), d8 with three unpaired electrons

q: Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii even though hafnium lies one period lower. What is the main reason?
why: Between Zr and Hf the 4f subshell is filled, and f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the effective nuclear charge rises and offsets the added shell. The equal valence electron count alone does not explain equal radii, since radii normally grow down a group.
opts: Poor shielding of the nuclear charge by the 4f electrons, giving the lanthanide contraction
The 5d electrons of hafnium shield the nucleus very effectively
Hafnium loses its 6s electrons more readily than zirconium loses its 5s electrons
Both elements have the same number of valence electrons and therefore equal radii

q: Arrange NaF, MgO, KCl and CaO in decreasing order of melting point.
why: Lattice energy scales with the product of charges over interionic distance. The doubly charged oxides are far above the singly charged halides, and the smaller Mg2+ gives MgO a higher value than CaO. Between the halides, the smaller ions of NaF give a larger lattice energy than KCl.

q: A 1.907 g sample of borax, Na2B4O7.10H2O (molar mass 381.4 g/mol), is dissolved and titrated with 0.100 M HCl. The reaction is Na2B4O7 + 2HCl + 5H2O -> 4H3BO3 + 2NaCl. What volume of HCl is required?
why: Moles of borax = 1.907/381.4 = 5.00 x 10^-3 mol. It consumes twice as many moles of HCl, 1.00 x 10^-2 mol, so the volume is 0.0100/0.100 = 0.100 L = 100 mL. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 50 mL.

q: Sodium peroxide reacts with carbon dioxide: 2Na2O2 + 2CO2 -> 2Na2CO3 + O2. What mass of oxygen is released from 7.8 g of Na2O2 (78 g/mol)? (O = 16 g/mol)
why: Moles of Na2O2 = 7.8/78 = 0.100 mol. The equation gives 1 mol O2 per 2 mol Na2O2, so 0.0500 mol O2 forms, which weighs 1.6 g. Taking one mole of O2 per mole of peroxide gives 3.2 g.

q: Chlorine is passed into hot concentrated NaOH solution: 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O. How many moles of NaCl form when 0.30 mol of Cl2 reacts completely?
why: Five NaCl form for every three Cl2, so NaCl = 0.30 x 5/3 = 0.50 mol. The value 0.30 mol corresponds to the cold dilute reaction (Cl2 -> NaCl + NaClO), and 0.10 mol is the NaClO3 amount.

q: A 50.0 mL sample of hard water needs 12.5 mL of 0.0100 M EDTA solution to reach the end point. Taking all hardness as Ca2+ expressed as CaCO3 (100 g/mol) and EDTA complexing Ca2+ in a 1:1 ratio, what is the hardness in ppm (mg per litre)?
why: Moles of EDTA = 0.0125 L x 0.0100 = 1.25 x 10^-4 mol, equal to moles of CaCO3, which is 12.5 mg. This is in 50.0 mL, so per litre it is 12.5 x 20 = 250 mg/L. Forgetting to scale from 50 mL to 1 L, or scaling by the wrong factor, gives the other choices.

q: How many of the following ions are colourless in aqueous solution: Ag+, Zn2+, Sc3+, Ti3+, Ti4+, V3+?
why: Colour in these ions comes from d-d transitions, which need a partly filled d subshell. Ag+ (d10), Zn2+ (d10), Sc3+ (d0) and Ti4+ (d0) have none, so they are colourless. Ti3+ (d1) is purple and V3+ (d2) is green, so the count is 4.

q: Arrange Cl2O, H2O and OF2 in increasing order of bond angle.
why: In OF2 the bonding pairs are pulled toward fluorine, away from oxygen, so lone-pair repulsion squeezes the angle to about 103 degrees. In H2O the angle is 104.5 degrees. In Cl2O the large Cl atoms repel each other sterically and the angle opens to about 111 degrees.

q: A 50.0 mL sample of 0.100 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.76) is mixed with 20.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. What is the pH of the resulting solution? (log 2 = 0.30, log 3 = 0.48)
why: Acid taken = 5.0 mmol, NaOH = 2.0 mmol, so 2.0 mmol acetate forms and 3.0 mmol acetic acid remains. pH = 4.76 + log(2.0/3.0) = 4.76 - 0.18 = 4.58. The value 4.94 results from inverting the ratio, and 4.76 would need equal amounts of acid and base.

q: The solubility product of AgCl is 1.8 x 10^-10 at 25 C. What is its molar solubility in 0.010 M NaCl solution?
why: The common ion fixes [Cl-] at about 0.010 M, so s = Ksp/[Cl-] = 1.8 x 10^-10 / 1.0 x 10^-2 = 1.8 x 10^-8 M. The figure 1.3 x 10^-5 M is the solubility in pure water (sqrt(Ksp)) and ignores the common ion.

q: The solubility product of Mg(OH)2 is 4.0 x 10^-12. What is the pH of its saturated solution in pure water (assume the OH- from water is negligible; log 2 = 0.30)?
why: With solubility s, Ksp = s x (2s)^2 = 4s^3, so s = 1.0 x 10^-4 M and [OH-] = 2s = 2.0 x 10^-4 M. pOH = 4 - 0.30 = 3.70, so pH = 10.30. Taking [OH-] = s gives 10.00, and 3.70 is the pOH, not the pH.

q: 5.85 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved in 500 g of water. The salt is 90 percent dissociated into ions. Taking Kf of water as 1.86 K kg/mol, the depression in freezing point is closest to
why: Molality = 0.100 mol / 0.500 kg = 0.200 mol/kg. The van't Hoff factor i = 1 + alpha = 1.90, so the depression = 1.90 x 1.86 x 0.200 = 0.71 K. Complete dissociation (i = 2) gives 0.74 K, and no dissociation gives 0.37 K.

q: A protein solution contains 1.0 g of protein in 100 mL of solution. Its osmotic pressure at 300 K is 2.46 x 10^-3 atm. Taking R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K), the molar mass of the protein is closest to
why: The concentration is 10 g/L, so M = cRT/pi = (10 x 0.0821 x 300)/(2.46 x 10^-3) = 1.0 x 10^5 g/mol. Using 1 g/L (forgetting that 100 mL is only one tenth of a litre) would give 1.0 x 10^4 g/mol.

q: A liquid mixture contains 2.0 mol of benzene and 3.0 mol of toluene and behaves ideally. At the given temperature the vapour pressures of pure benzene and pure toluene are 75 torr and 22 torr. What is the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour in equilibrium with the liquid?
why: Liquid mole fractions are 0.4 and 0.6. Partial pressures: benzene 0.4 x 75 = 30 torr, toluene 0.6 x 22 = 13.2 torr, total 43.2 torr. Vapour mole fraction of benzene = 30/43.2 = 0.69. The value 0.40 is just the liquid composition, which ignores benzene's greater volatility.

q: The solubility of pure oxygen in water at 1 atm is 1.3 x 10^-3 mol/L at a given temperature. Air contains 21 percent oxygen by volume. What is the dissolved oxygen concentration in water in equilibrium with air at a total pressure of 2.0 atm?
why: By Henry's law the concentration is proportional to the partial pressure of O2, which is 0.21 x 2.0 = 0.42 atm. Concentration = 1.3 x 10^-3 x 0.42 = 5.5 x 10^-4 M. Using 1 atm of air (0.21 atm of O2) gives 2.7 x 10^-4 M, forgetting the doubled total pressure.

q: A metal of molar mass 27 g/mol and density 2.70 g/cm^3 crystallises in a face-centred cubic lattice. Taking N_A = 6.02 x 10^23 /mol, the edge of the unit cell is closest to
why: fcc has 4 atoms per cell, so a^3 = 4 x 27/(6.02 x 10^23 x 2.70) = 6.6 x 10^-23 cm^3 and a = 4.05 x 10^-8 cm = 405 pm. Taking a body-centred cell (2 atoms) gives 321 pm and a simple cubic cell (1 atom) gives 255 pm.

q: In a solid, the anions X form a cubic close-packed lattice and the cations M occupy two thirds of the octahedral holes. If X is a divalent anion, the oxidation state of M is
why: A ccp lattice has 4 anions and 4 octahedral holes per cell. Cations fill 2/3 of 4 holes, so M : X = (8/3) : 4 = 2 : 3 and the formula is M2X3. Charge balance with X as 2- gives 2 x (M) = 6, so M is +3.

q: In the adsorption of a gas on charcoal at constant temperature, 2.0 mg of gas per gram is adsorbed at 0.10 atm and 4.0 mg per gram at 0.40 atm, and the data fit x/m = k P^(1/n). The amount adsorbed per gram at 0.90 atm is
why: Pressure rises 4 times while the amount doubles, so 4^(1/n) = 2 and 1/n = 0.5. Then x/m at 0.90 atm = 2.0 x (0.90/0.10)^0.5 = 2.0 x 3 = 6.0 mg. A linear (direct proportion) assumption would give 18 mg from the first point or 9.0 mg from the second.

q: A positively charged Fe(OH)3 sol is to be coagulated. Equal molar concentrations of four electrolytes are tried. Which one will bring about coagulation at the lowest concentration?
why: Coagulation is brought about by the ion of charge opposite to that on the colloid, and its power rises steeply with that charge (Hardy-Schulze rule). For a positive sol the anion matters, and PO4^3- is trivalent, more effective than SO4^2- or Cl-. The tempting BaCl2 has a divalent cation, which has the same sign as the sol and so is ineffective.

q: Unpolluted rain water is in equilibrium with atmospheric CO2 and contains dissolved CO2 (as H2CO3) at 1.0 x 10^-5 M. Taking the first dissociation constant of H2CO3 as 4.0 x 10^-7 and ignoring all other equilibria, the pH of the rain is closest to (log 2 = 0.30)
why: For a weak acid [H+] = sqrt(Ka x C) = sqrt(4.0 x 10^-7 x 1.0 x 10^-5) = 2.0 x 10^-6 M, so pH = 6 - 0.30 = 5.70. Taking [H+] = Ka gives 6.40, taking [H+] = C gives 5.00, and taking sqrt(Ka) gives 3.20.

q: Temporary hardness in 10.0 L of water is due to 1.62 g of Ca(HCO3)2 (molar mass 162 g/mol). In Clark's method, slaked lime Ca(OH)2 (molar mass 74 g/mol) is added to precipitate CaCO3. What mass of Ca(OH)2 is needed?
why: Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 gives 2 CaCO3 + 2 H2O, a 1 : 1 ratio. Moles of Ca(HCO3)2 = 1.62/162 = 0.0100, so Ca(OH)2 = 0.0100 mol = 0.74 g. Assuming 2 mol of lime per mole of bicarbonate gives 1.48 g.

q: 25.0 mL of an oxalic acid solution is titrated in acidic medium with 0.100 M KMnO4, of which 20.0 mL is needed to reach the end point. The molarity of the oxalic acid is
why: 5 H2C2O4 + 2 MnO4- react, so mol oxalic acid = 2.5 x mol MnO4-. MnO4- = 0.100 x 20.0 = 2.00 mmol, so oxalic acid = 5.00 mmol and its molarity = 5.00/25.0 = 0.200 M. Treating the normality 0.400 N as molarity gives 0.400 M, and a 1 : 1 ratio gives 0.080 M.

q: 0.500 g of an impure sample of CaCO3 is treated with 50.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl (impurities do not react with the acid). The excess acid needs 20.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. The percentage of CaCO3 in the sample is (molar mass 100 g/mol)
why: HCl taken = 10.0 mmol and excess = 2.0 mmol, so 8.0 mmol reacted. CaCO3 + 2 HCl, hence CaCO3 = 4.0 mmol = 0.400 g, which is 80 percent of 0.500 g. Ignoring the back-titration gives 100 percent, and using only the excess gives 20 percent.

q: What is the pH of a 0.10 M solution of NH4Cl? Kb of NH3 = 1.8 x 10^-5 and Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14 (take log 7.45 = 0.87).
why: The NH4+ ion is a weak acid with Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 x 10^-10. [H+] = sqrt(Ka x 0.10) = 7.5 x 10^-6 M, so pH = 5.13. The salt of a weak base and strong acid is acidic, so 8.87 is wrong, and 2.87 arises from using Kb directly in sqrt(Kb x C).

q: A solution contains 0.010 M Cl- and 0.010 M CrO4^2-. Solid AgNO3 is added gradually (no volume change). Ksp of AgCl = 1.8 x 10^-10 and Ksp of Ag2CrO4 = 1.1 x 10^-12. When Ag2CrO4 just begins to precipitate, the concentration of Cl- left in solution is closest to
why: Ag2CrO4 starts to form when [Ag+] = sqrt(1.1 x 10^-12/0.010) = 1.05 x 10^-5 M. At that [Ag+], [Cl-] = 1.8 x 10^-10 / 1.05 x 10^-5 = 1.7 x 10^-5 M, so AgCl has precipitated almost completely first. The 1.0 x 10^-5 M option is just the silver ion concentration.

q: 6.0 g of acetic acid (molar mass 60 g/mol) is dissolved in 100 g of benzene (Kf = 5.12 K kg/mol). The acid dimerises in benzene and the observed depression in freezing point is 2.816 K. The degree of association is
why: Without association the depression would be 1.00 mol/kg x 5.12 = 5.12 K, so i = 2.816/5.12 = 0.55. For dimerisation 2A gives A2, i = 1 - alpha/2, so alpha = 2(1 - 0.55) = 0.90. The values 0.45 (1 - i) and 0.55 (i itself) are common slips.

q: A 2.00 M aqueous solution of H2SO4 (molar mass 98 g/mol) has a density of 1.12 g/mL. Its molality is closest to
why: In 1 L of solution: mass = 1120 g and H2SO4 = 2 x 98 = 196 g, so water = 924 g = 0.924 kg. Molality = 2.00/0.924 = 2.16 mol/kg. Dividing by the density (2.00/1.12) gives the wrong 1.79 m, and 2.00 m would need the solvent to weigh exactly 1 kg.

q: 1.0 L of a buffer contains 0.20 mol NH3 and 0.20 mol NH4Cl (pKb of NH3 = 4.74, so pKa of NH4+ = 9.26). After 0.050 mol of HCl is added (no volume change), the pH is closest to (log 0.6 = -0.22)
why: HCl converts NH3 to NH4+, leaving 0.15 mol NH3 and 0.25 mol NH4+. pH = 9.26 + log(0.15/0.25) = 9.26 - 0.22 = 9.04. Placing the acid in the numerator gives 9.48, and 9.26 ignores the addition. The value 8.78 would correspond to adding 0.10 mol of HCl.

q: Phosphoric acid has pKa values of 2.15, 7.20 and 12.35. The pH of a dilute solution of the amphiprotic salt Na2HPO4 is closest to
why: HPO4^2- can both accept and donate a proton, so pH = (pKa2 + pKa3)/2 = (7.20 + 12.35)/2 = 9.78. The value 4.68 is for NaH2PO4 (average of pKa1 and pKa2), and 7.20 would be the pH of an equimolar H2PO4- / HPO4^2- buffer.

q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the chemisorption of hydrogen on nickel, in comparison with the physisorption of nitrogen on charcoal at low temperature?
why: Chemisorption involves bond formation, so its enthalpy is large, it is confined to a monolayer, it is specific and it can need activation energy. The option with multilayers and easy reversal by lowering pressure describes physisorption, but gives it the large enthalpy of chemisorption, so it mixes the two.
opts: The enthalpy of adsorption is small (about -20 to -40 kJ/mol) and multilayers can form
The enthalpy of adsorption is large (about -80 to -240 kJ/mol), multilayers form and the process is easily reversed by lowering the pressure
The enthalpy of adsorption is small (about -20 to -40 kJ/mol), only a monolayer forms and the extent of adsorption rises steadily with temperature
The enthalpy of adsorption is large (about -80 to -240 kJ/mol), the layer is at most one molecule thick, some activation energy is needed and the process is specific to the surface

q: A water sample contains only 18 mg/L of glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180 g/mol) as the oxidisable pollutant. If it is completely oxidised to CO2 and H2O, the theoretical oxygen demand is (O = 16)
why: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 gives 6 CO2 + 6 H2O. Glucose = 18 mg/180 = 0.10 mmol/L, so O2 needed = 0.60 mmol/L = 0.60 x 32 = 19.2 mg/L. Counting oxygen atoms (16) rather than O2 molecules gives 9.6 mg/L.

q: The solubility product of Al(OH)3 is 1.0 x 10^-33. The molar concentration of Al3+ that can remain dissolved in a solution buffered at pH 4.00 is
why: At pH 4.00, [OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-10 M. Ksp = [Al3+][OH-]^3, so [Al3+] = 10^-33 / 10^-30 = 1.0 x 10^-3 M. Using [OH-]^2 gives 10^-13, using [OH-]^1 gives 10^-23, and mistaking pH 4 for pOH 4 gives 10^-21.

q: A 0.90 percent (mass/volume) NaCl solution (9.0 g/L, molar mass 58.5 g/mol, assume complete dissociation) is used as a reference. What mass of urea (molar mass 60 g/mol) per litre will give a solution isotonic with it at the same temperature?
why: NaCl is 9.0/58.5 = 0.154 mol/L giving 2 x 0.154 = 0.308 mol/L of particles. Urea does not dissociate, so it needs 0.308 mol/L x 60 = 18.5 g/L. Forgetting the factor of 2 for NaCl gives 9.2 g/L.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2CHCH2CH(OH)CH3?
why: The longest chain containing the carbon bearing OH has five carbons. Numbering from the end that gives OH the lowest locant puts OH on C2 and the methyl on C4, so the name is 4-methylpentan-2-ol. 2-Methylpentan-4-ol fails because the principal group must receive the lowest number, not the substituent.

q: How many isomers in total, counting cis and trans forms separately, exist for compounds of formula C4H8 that are either alkenes or cycloalkanes (a single ring, no further stereoisomers from the ring)?
why: Alkenes: but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene give 4. The rings cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane add 2 more, giving 6. The tempting answer 4 forgets the cycloalkanes, which have the same formula CnH2n.

q: Which of the following alkyl bromides reacts fastest with sodium iodide in dry acetone?
why: Sodium iodide in acetone is a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, so the SN2 path dominates and the rate falls with crowding at the carbon attacked. The unhindered primary bromide is fastest. 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is tempting through SN1 thinking, but SN1 is not favoured here and backside attack on a tertiary carbon is blocked.

q: In a solvolysis that follows a pure SN1 mechanism, the concentration of the alkyl halide is doubled and the concentration of the added nucleophile is tripled (solvent unchanged). By what factor does the rate change?
why: The slow step of SN1 is ionisation of the alkyl halide alone, so rate = k[RX]. Doubling [RX] doubles the rate, and the nucleophile concentration does not appear in the rate law. A six-fold change would be right only for an SN2 reaction that is first order in each reactant.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol. What is the major alkene formed?
why: With a very bulky base E2 removes the most accessible hydrogen, here from the CH3 group, so the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product) 2-methylbut-1-ene predominates. 2-Methylbut-2-ene is the Zaitsev product seen with a small base such as ethoxide, which is the tempting choice. 3-Methylbut-1-ene cannot form from this skeleton and 2-methylbut-3-ene is not a valid name.

q: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr in the absence of peroxides. What is the major product?
why: Protonation at C1 gives a secondary carbocation at C2, next to a quaternary carbon. A methyl group shifts from C3 to C2, giving a more stable tertiary cation, and bromide attacks it to give 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. 2-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane is the tempting unrearranged Markovnikov product.

q: Which compound gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide solution?
why: The iodoform test needs a CH3-CO- group or a CH3-CH(OH)- group that can be oxidised to it in situ. 1-Phenylethanol contains CH3CH(OH)- attached to the ring and gives CHI3. Pentan-3-one has only CH2 groups next to the carbonyl, and propan-1-ol and benzaldehyde have no methyl carbinol or methyl ketone unit.

q: Which order correctly lists the compounds in increasing rate of electrophilic nitration?
why: The nitro group strongly withdraws electrons and deactivates most, chlorine deactivates weakly through its inductive effect (though it directs ortho and para), benzene is the reference, and the methyl group activates by hyperconjugation and induction. This gives nitrobenzene < chlorobenzene < benzene < toluene. Placing chlorobenzene above benzene confuses its ortho/para direction with activation.

q: How many optically active stereoisomers are possible in total for an open-chain aldohexose (all stereocentres counted, enantiomers counted separately)?
why: An open-chain aldohexose CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CHO has four stereocentres, C2 to C5, and no internal symmetry, so there are 2^4 = 16 stereoisomers. 32 comes from wrongly counting five centres (including C6), and 8 from counting only three.

q: How many stereoisomers does pent-3-en-2-ol, CH3CH=CHCH(OH)CH3, have in total?
why: C2 is a chiral centre, giving R and S forms. The double bond has different groups on both ends (CH3 and H on one carbon, CH(OH)CH3 and H on the other), so E and Z forms exist. These independent features give 2 x 2 = 4 stereoisomers; answering 2 counts only one feature.

q: A sample of 1.20 g of a dicarboxylic acid is exactly neutralised by 40.0 mL of 0.50 mol/L sodium hydroxide. What is its molar mass in g/mol?
why: Moles of NaOH = 0.0400 L x 0.50 = 0.020 mol. Each molecule of the dibasic acid uses 2 NaOH, so moles of acid = 0.010 mol and M = 1.20/0.010 = 120 g/mol. The tempting 60 g/mol treats the acid as monobasic.

q: Methanal is mixed with benzaldehyde in concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. Which pair of products mainly forms?
why: Neither aldehyde has an alpha hydrogen, so a crossed Cannizzaro reaction occurs. The hydroxide adduct of the more electrophilic methanal is the better hydride donor and is oxidised to methanoate, while benzaldehyde accepts the hydride and is reduced to benzyl alcohol. Sodium benzoate and methanol would be the reverse role assignment.
opts: sodium benzoate and benzyl alcohol only

q: Benzene is treated with 1-chloropropane and anhydrous aluminium chloride. Which is the major product?
why: AlCl3 ionises the primary halide towards a primary carbocation character, which undergoes a hydride shift to the more stable secondary propan-2-yl cation before attacking the ring. The major product is propan-2-ylbenzene. Propylbenzene is the tempting direct-substitution answer and is only minor.

q: Which sequence lists the compounds in increasing acid strength?
why: Alcohols are far weaker acids than phenols because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation. Within phenols, the electron-donating methyl group destabilises the anion (p-cresol is weaker than phenol) and the nitro group stabilises it strongly. The order is ethanol < p-cresol < phenol < p-nitrophenol; putting p-cresol above phenol ignores the donor effect of methyl.

q: An alkene of general formula CnH2n weighing 2.80 g reacts exactly with 8.0 g of bromine (Br2 = 160 g/mol) in an addition reaction. What is its molecular formula?
why: Moles of Br2 = 8.0/160 = 0.050 mol, and one mole of alkene takes one mole of Br2, so the molar mass is 2.80/0.050 = 56 g/mol. For CnH2n, 14n = 56 so n = 4, giving C4H8. Using 80 g/mol for Br2 would give 28 g/mol and the wrong answer C2H4.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide by a pure SN2 mechanism. What is the main substitution product?
why: SN2 proceeds with backside attack and inversion of the spatial arrangement. Here the priorities are unchanged (the new OH ranks first just as Br did), so the descriptor changes from R to S, giving (S)-butan-2-ol. Retention or a racemic mixture would indicate an SN1 path.

q: How many different tripeptides can be formed from three different amino acids when each amino acid is used exactly once in each tripeptide?
why: The tripeptides differ in the sequence of the three amino acids along the chain, so the number equals the permutations of three distinct units, 3! = 6. Answering 3 counts only the choice of the N-terminal residue and ignores order of the rest.

q: Ethyl ethanoate is hydrolysed in dilute acid using water that is enriched in oxygen-18. Where does the label appear?
why: Ester hydrolysis proceeds by attack of water on the protonated carbonyl carbon and cleavage of the acyl-oxygen bond (C-OEt), so the oxygen of water ends up in the carboxylic acid. The ethanol keeps the oxygen it had in the ester and carries no label. The tempting ethanol option applies to alkyl-oxygen cleavage, which does not happen here.
opts: in the ethanoic acid, with no label in the ethanol
equally in ethanol and ethanoic acid

q: Ethanal (44 g/mol) is oxidised completely by Tollens reagent and 5.4 g of silver (108 g/mol) is deposited. What mass of ethanal reacted?
why: Moles of Ag = 5.4/108 = 0.050 mol. Each ethanal gives two Ag (the aldehyde group loses two electrons), so moles of ethanal = 0.025 mol and mass = 0.025 x 44 = 1.1 g. The value 2.2 g results from assuming a one-to-one ratio.

q: How many moles of H2 are consumed per mole of benzaldehyde when it is completely hydrogenated over a nickel catalyst at high temperature and pressure to give cyclohexylmethanol?
why: The aromatic ring takes three moles of H2 (three C=C equivalents) and the aldehyde C=O takes one more to become CH2OH, a total of four. Answering 1 counts only the carbonyl and 3 counts only the ring.

q: Which of the following benzyl chlorides undergoes SN1 solvolysis in aqueous ethanol most rapidly?
why: The rate is controlled by the stability of the benzyl cation. The methoxy group in the para position donates electrons by resonance and strongly stabilises the cation. The nitro group destabilises it, and chlorine, mainly an inductive acceptor, is slightly worse than hydrogen. Benzyl chloride is only the reference rate.

q: Ethanoic acid (1.0 mol) and ethanol (2.0 mol) react in a mixture where the equilibrium constant for ester formation is 4.0 (volume cancels because the number of moles of reactants and products is equal). How many moles of ester are present at equilibrium?
why: Let x be the moles of ester. Then x^2/[(1-x)(2-x)] = 4, which gives 3x^2 - 12x + 8 = 0 and x = (12 - sqrt(48))/6 = 0.85 mol (the other root exceeds 1). The value 0.67 is what an equimolar mixture (1.0 mol of each) would give, ignoring the excess ethanol.

q: Which pair of reactants, followed by acidic work-up, gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
why: A tertiary alcohol arises from a ketone plus a Grignard reagent. Propanone with CH3MgBr gives (CH3)3COH after hydrolysis, which is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Ethanal gives secondary alcohols (propan-2-ol or butan-2-ol) and methanal gives a primary alcohol (2-methylpropan-1-ol here).

q: Butan-2-ol is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid at 440 K. Which is the major organic product?
why: E1 type elimination through the secondary cation follows the Zaitsev rule and gives the more substituted but-2-ene, and the trans isomer is more stable than the cis because of less steric strain. But-1-ene is the minor product and 2-methylpropene would need a skeletal rearrangement that does not occur here.

q: Sucrose does not reduce Tollens reagent. What is the reason?
why: In sucrose the glycosidic bond joins C1 of glucose with C2 of fructose, so both anomeric carbons are acetal or ketal carbons and cannot open to give a free carbonyl group. Sucrose has many hydroxyl groups, and fructose itself reduces Tollens reagent through the alpha-hydroxy ketone, so the ketone character is not the reason.
opts: both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, leaving no free aldehyde or hemiacetal group
it is a ketose with no alpha-hydroxy ketone
the glucose unit is present in the furanose ring form

q: A 1.000 g mixture of Na2CO3 and NaHCO3 is heated strongly until the bicarbonate is fully converted to the carbonate (2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2). The mass of the solid falls by 0.155 g. Taking molar masses NaHCO3 = 84 and Na2CO3 = 106 g/mol, what is the mass percentage of NaHCO3 in the original mixture?
why: Two moles of NaHCO3 (168 g) lose 62 g (H2O + CO2), so mass of NaHCO3 = 0.155 x 168/62 = 0.420 g, i.e. 42%. Using 84 g per 62 g, as if only one mole were involved, gives the tempting 21%; 58% is just the Na2CO3 share.

q: In acidic solution, MnO4^- is reduced to Mn2+ and Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+. What volume of 0.20 M KMnO4 is needed to oxidise completely 25 mL of 0.50 M FeSO4?
why: Fe2+ = 25 x 0.50 = 12.5 mmol. Each MnO4^- takes 5 electrons, so it oxidises 5 Fe2+; MnO4^- needed = 12.5/5 = 2.5 mmol, volume = 2.5/0.20 = 12.5 mL. The tempting 62.5 mL comes from multiplying by 5 instead of dividing.

q: 10 mL of a gaseous hydrocarbon is burnt in excess oxygen. After the products are cooled to room temperature (liquid water), the total volume has contracted by 25 mL; passing the gas through KOH solution then reduces the volume by a further 30 mL. All volumes are at the same temperature and pressure. The hydrocarbon is
why: The KOH absorbs CO2: 30 mL from 10 mL gives x = 3. For CxHy the contraction on combustion is (1 + y/4) per unit volume of hydrocarbon, so 10(1 + y/4) = 25 and y = 6. The formula is C3H6; C3H8 would give a contraction of 30 mL.

q: The Bohr energy of the n-th level of a hydrogen-like ion is -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. What is the energy of the photon emitted when the electron of Li2+ (Z = 3) falls from n = 2 to n = 1?
why: Energy = 13.6 x 9 x (1/1 - 1/4) = 122.4 x 0.75 = 91.8 eV. Forgetting the (1 - 1/4) factor gives 122.4 eV, and 40.8 eV is the value for He+ (Z = 2).

q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 150 V. Take h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, electron mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C. Its de Broglie wavelength is closest to
why: Kinetic energy = eV, so p = sqrt(2 m e V) = sqrt(2 x 9.1e-31 x 1.6e-19 x 150) = 6.6e-24 kg m/s and wavelength = h/p = 1.0e-10 m = 100 pm. Leaving out the factor 2 under the root gives 142 pm.

q: How many electrons in a ground-state chromium atom (Z = 24) have the magnetic quantum number m_l = 0?
why: Chromium is [Ar] 3d5 4s1. Every s electron has m_l = 0: 2+2+2+1 = 7 (1s, 2s, 3s, 4s). In each p subshell one orbital has m_l = 0: 2 electrons each in 2p and 3p = 4. In 3d, with five singly occupied orbitals, one electron has m_l = 0. Total = 7 + 4 + 1 = 12. Using 4s2 instead of 4s1 gives the tempting 13.

q: A closed vessel contains equal masses of methane (CH4, 16 g/mol) and oxygen (O2, 32 g/mol) at 300 K, and the total pressure is 1.50 atm. The partial pressure of oxygen is
why: For mass m of each, moles CH4 = m/16 and moles O2 = m/32, so the mole fraction of O2 = (1/32)/(1/16 + 1/32) = 1/3. Partial pressure = 1.50/3 = 0.50 atm. Equal masses do not mean equal moles, so 0.75 atm is wrong.

q: At 300 K the root mean square speed of H2 molecules is v. At what temperature will O2 molecules have the same root mean square speed v? (H = 1, O = 16)
why: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), so equal speeds need T/M equal: T = 300 x 32/2 = 4800 K. Taking the square root of the mass ratio by mistake gives 1200 K, and inverting the ratio gives about 19 K.

q: Equal volumes of SO2 (64 g/mol) and an unknown gas X, at the same temperature and pressure, are allowed to effuse separately through the same small hole. X takes 20 s and SO2 takes 40 s. The molar mass of X is
why: Time is proportional to sqrt(M): t_X/t_SO2 = sqrt(M_X/64) = 20/40 = 1/2, so M_X/64 = 1/4 and M_X = 16 g/mol. Forgetting to square the ratio gives 32 g/mol.

q: The standard enthalpies of combustion at 298 K are: graphite -393.5 kJ/mol, H2(g) -285.8 kJ/mol and CH4(g) -890.3 kJ/mol. The standard enthalpy of formation of CH4(g) is
why: C + 2H2 -> CH4: dHf = dHc(C) + 2 dHc(H2) - dHc(CH4) = -393.5 - 571.6 + 890.3 = -74.8 kJ/mol. Counting only one H2 (instead of two) gives +211.0 kJ/mol.

q: For a reaction dH = +40.0 kJ/mol and dS = +100 J/(mol K), and both may be treated as independent of temperature. Above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous?
why: dG = dH - T dS = 0 at T = 40000 J/mol / 100 J/(mol K) = 400 K. Using dH in kJ with dS in J without conversion gives the tempting 0.40 K, and 4000 K comes from a slip of a factor of 10 in the same step.

q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g) at 300 K, dH = -92.0 kJ per mole of reaction. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol K). The internal energy change dU for the reaction as written is closest to
why: dU = dH - (dn_g)RT with dn_g = 2 - 4 = -2, so dU = -92.0 + 2 x 8.314 x 300/1000 = -92.0 + 5.0 = -87.0 kJ. Using dn_g = -1 gives -89.5 kJ, and the wrong sign of the correction gives -97.0 kJ.

q: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas (Cv = 3R/2) at 300 K and 4.0 atm expands adiabatically against a constant external pressure of 1.0 atm until its pressure is 1.0 atm. The final temperature is
why: For the irreversible process q = 0, so n Cv (T2 - T1) = -P_ext(V2 - V1). With V2 = RT2/1 and V1 = R(300)/4: 1.5(T2 - 300) = -(T2 - 75), giving 2.5 T2 = 525 and T2 = 210 K. The reversible adiabatic formula (300 x 4^-0.4 = 172 K) wrongly applies to this irreversible case.

q: PCl5(g) is placed in a vessel and, at equilibrium, is 40% dissociated (PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2) at a total pressure of 2.0 atm. The value of Kp is closest to
why: Starting with 1 mol: PCl5 = 0.6, PCl3 = Cl2 = 0.4, total 1.4 mol. Kp = (0.4/1.4 x 2)^2 / (0.6/1.4 x 2) = (0.571)^2/0.857 = 0.381 atm. Using (1 - alpha) in the denominator instead of (1 - alpha^2) in alpha^2 P/(1 - alpha^2) leads to 0.53 atm.

q: 100 mL of 0.10 M NH3 (Kb = 1.8 x 10^-5, so pKb = 4.74) is mixed with 40 mL of 0.10 M HCl. Take pKw = 14. The pH of the resulting solution is closest to
why: NH3 = 10 mmol - 4 mmol = 6 mmol left, NH4+ formed = 4 mmol, a basic buffer. pOH = pKb + log(NH4+/NH3) = 4.74 + log(4/6) = 4.57, so pH = 14 - 4.57 = 9.43. Inverting the ratio gives 9.08, and 4.57 is the pOH, not the pH.

q: The Ksp of Ag2CrO4 is 4.0 x 10^-12 at 25 C. Its solubility in 0.010 M K2CrO4 solution (assume the chromate concentration is essentially 0.010 M) is
why: Ksp = [Ag+]^2[CrO4^2-] = (2s)^2 x 0.010 = 0.04 s^2, so s^2 = 1.0 x 10^-10 and s = 1.0 x 10^-5 M. Omitting the factor 2 in [Ag+] gives 2.0 x 10^-5, and 1.0 x 10^-4 M is the solubility in pure water.

q: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), Kc = 100 L/mol at 800 K. Taking R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K), the value of Kp (in atm^-1) is closest to
why: Kp = Kc (RT)^dn with dn = 2 - 3 = -1, so Kp = 100/(0.0821 x 800) = 100/65.7 = 1.52 atm^-1. Multiplying by RT instead of dividing gives 6.6 x 10^3, and 100 is Kc itself.

q: A first-order reaction is 75% complete in 40 minutes. How long, from the start, does it take to be 93.75% complete?
why: 75% complete means two half-lives, so t1/2 = 20 min. 93.75% complete means 6.25% = 1/16 remains, which is four half-lives, i.e. 80 min. 60 min would correspond to three half-lives (87.5% complete).

q: For a certain reaction the rate doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol K) and ln 2 = 0.693. The activation energy is closest to
why: ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 - 1/T2) = (Ea/R)(10/(300 x 310)), so Ea = 8.314 x 0.693 x 9300 = 53.6 kJ/mol. Slips of a factor of 10 or of 2 in this arithmetic lead to 5.4 or 107 kJ/mol, and 26.8 kJ/mol results from halving.

q: In a reaction A + B -> products, doubling [A] at fixed [B] quadruples the rate, and doubling [B] at fixed [A] doubles the rate. When [A] = 0.10 M and [B] = 0.10 M the rate is 2.0 x 10^-4 M/s. What is the rate when [A] = 0.30 M and [B] = 0.20 M?
why: The rate law is rate = k[A]^2[B]. Tripling [A] multiplies the rate by 9 and doubling [B] by 2, so the new rate = 2.0 x 10^-4 x 18 = 3.6 x 10^-3 M/s. Treating the reaction as first order in each reactant gives 1.2 x 10^-3.

q: The gas A decomposes at constant volume and temperature by a first-order process: A(g) -> 2B(g) + C(g). The initial pressure is 100 mm Hg (pure A) and after 20 min the total pressure is 160 mm Hg. The rate constant is closest to
why: If p of A has reacted, the total is 100 - p + 3p = 100 + 2p = 160, so p = 30 and A left = 70 mm Hg. k = (1/20) ln(100/70) = 1.78 x 10^-2 per min. Using the total pressure ratio 160/100 gives 2.35 x 10^-2, and assuming 40 mm Hg of A remained gives 4.58 x 10^-2.

q: The same current is passed in series through two cells, one containing AgNO3 solution and the other CuSO4 solution (both with inert electrodes). 1.08 g of silver is deposited. Taking Ag = 108 and Cu = 63.5, the mass of copper deposited is
why: Silver: 1.08/108 = 0.0100 mol, so 0.0100 mol of electrons passed. Cu2+ takes 2 electrons per Cu, giving 0.00500 mol = 0.318 g. Forgetting that copper needs two electrons gives 0.635 g.

q: A cell consists of a Zn electrode in 0.010 M Zn2+ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M Cu2+, joined by a salt bridge. The standard cell emf is 1.10 V. Use E = E0 - (0.0592/n) log Q at 298 K. The cell emf is
Standard reduction potentials are Fe3+/Fe2+ = +0.77 V and Sn4+/Sn2+ = +0.15 V. At 298 K the equilibrium constant of Sn2+ + 2Fe3+ <=> Sn4+ + 2Fe2+ is closest to (use log K = nE0/0.0592)
why: E0 cell = 0.77 - 0.15 = 0.62 V and n = 2, so log K = 2 x 0.62/0.0592 = 20.95 and K = 9 x 10^20. Using n = 1 gives 3 x 10^10, and using n = 4 gives 8 x 10^41.

q: The conductivity of a 0.10 M solution of a weak monobasic acid HA is 1.0 x 10^-3 S/cm. The limiting molar conductivity of HA is 400 S cm^2/mol. The dissociation constant Ka of the acid is closest to
why: Molar conductivity = 1000 x 1.0e-3/0.10 = 10 S cm^2/mol, so alpha = 10/400 = 0.025. Ka = C alpha^2/(1 - alpha) = 0.10 x 6.25e-4/0.975 = 6.4 x 10^-5. The value 2.5 x 10^-3 results from using C x alpha instead of C x alpha^2.

q: The roots of x^2 - 9x + 4 = 0 are a and b. Find a^2 + b^2.
why: Sum of roots is 9 and product is 4. Then a^2 + b^2 = (a+b)^2 - 2ab = 81 - 8 = 73.

q: An arithmetic sequence has first term 4 and common difference 3. Find the smallest positive integer n for which the sum of its first n terms exceeds 500.
why: The sum of the first n terms is n(3n+5)/2. For n = 17 this is 17*56/2 = 476, which is below 500, and for n = 18 it is 18*59/2 = 531, which exceeds 500.

q: Real numbers x and y satisfy x + 2y = 17 and 3x - y = 9. Find x^2 + y^2.
why: Eliminate y: y = 3x - 9, so x + 6x - 18 = 17 and x = 5, y = 6. Then x^2 + y^2 = 25 + 36 = 61.

q: A polynomial p(x) leaves remainder 5 when divided by x - 1 and remainder 11 when divided by x - 2. When p(x) is divided by (x-1)(x-2) the remainder has the form ax + b. Find the value of this remainder at x = 10.
why: The remainder theorem gives a + b = 5 and 2a + b = 11, so a = 6 and b = -1. At x = 10 the remainder equals 60 - 1 = 59.

q: The roots of x^3 - 7x^2 + 3x - 1 = 0 are a, b and c. Find the remainder when a^3 + b^3 + c^3 is divided by 100.
why: By Vieta, a+b+c = 7, ab+bc+ca = 3, abc = 1. The identity a^3+b^3+c^3 = (a+b+c)^3 - 3(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca) + 3abc gives 343 - 63 + 3 = 283, with remainder 83 on division by 100.

q: Find the number of ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfying 3x + 5y <= 40.
why: For each y from 1 to 7, the number of positive integers x with 3x <= 40 - 5y is floor((40-5y)/3). Adding these seven counts gives the total.

q: Non-negative integers x and y satisfy 5x + 7y <= 59. Find the largest possible value of 6x + 9y.
why: The objective gains 6/5 per unit of the constraint from x and 9/7 from y, so y is more efficient and the best points have y large. Checking y = 8, 7, 6, ... with the largest allowed x for each, and comparing the values of 6x + 9y, settles it. The maximum is 75 at (x, y) = (2, 7).

q: A sequence is defined by a_1 = 1 and a_(n+1) = 2a_n + 3. Find the remainder when a_10 is divided by 100.
why: Adding 3 to both sides gives a_(n+1) + 3 = 2(a_n + 3), so a_n + 3 = 4*2^(n-1) = 2^(n+1). Hence a_10 = 2^11 - 3 = 2045, with remainder 45.

q: Evaluate the sum of 1/(sqrt(k) + sqrt(k+1)) over k = 1, 2, ..., 99.
why: Rationalise each term: 1/(sqrt(k)+sqrt(k+1)) = sqrt(k+1) - sqrt(k). The sum telescopes to sqrt(100) - sqrt(1) = 9.

q: A function f is defined for all non-zero real numbers and satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 6x for every x. Find f(1/2).
A function f on the positive integers satisfies f(1) = 3 and f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n) + mn for all positive integers m and n. Find f(11).
P(x) is a monic cubic polynomial with P(1) = 1, P(2) = 2 and P(3) = 3. Find P(6).
why: Consider P(x) - x, a monic cubic vanishing at 1, 2 and 3. So P(x) = x + (x-1)(x-2)(x-3), and P(6) = 6 + 5*4*3 = 66.

q: Find the number of integers m for which the equation x^2 + mx + 360 = 0 has two integer roots (not necessarily distinct).
why: The roots p and q are integers with pq = 360, and m = -(p+q). The number 360 has 24 positive divisors, giving 12 unordered positive factor pairs, and the same number with both factors negative. All the sums are distinct, giving 24 values of m.

q: Positive integers x, y, z satisfy x + y + z = 13. Find the largest possible value of xyz.
why: The product is largest when the numbers are as equal as possible (AM-GM with integer adjustment): 4, 4, 5, giving 80.

q: A sequence has a_1 = 2, a_2 = 3 and a_(n+2) = a_(n+1) + a_n for all n >= 1. Find a_9.
why: Compute the terms: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89. The ninth term is 89.

q: Real numbers x, y, z satisfy x + y + z = 9, x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 29 and x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 99. Find the remainder when x^4 + y^4 + z^4 is divided by 100.
why: Newton's identities give xy+yz+zx = 26 and then xyz = 24 from the cubic sum, so x, y, z are the roots of t^3 - 9t^2 + 26t - 24 = 0, i.e. 2, 3, 4. Then x^4+y^4+z^4 = 16+81+256 = 353, with remainder 53.

q: Find the number of ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfying 1/x + 1/y = 1/12.
why: Rewrite as (x-12)(y-12) = 144. Both factors must be positive (since x, y > 12), so the count is the number of positive divisors of 144, which is 15.

q: Find the value of floor(1/3) + floor(2/3) + floor(3/3) + ... + floor(20/3), where floor(t) is the greatest integer not exceeding t.
why: Group the values by their floor: 0 occurs twice, each of 1 to 5 occurs three times (n up to 17), and 6 occurs three times (n = 18, 19, 20). The sum is 3(1+2+3+4+5+6) = 63.

q: Find the number of integers n for which n^2 - 20n + 51 < 0.
why: The quadratic factors as (n-3)(n-17), which is negative exactly when 3 < n < 17, so n = 4, 5, ..., 16.

q: The roots of x^2 - x - 1 = 0 are a and b. Find a^6 + b^6.
why: Let p_n = a^n + b^n. Then p_1 = 1, p_2 = 3 and p_(n+2) = p_(n+1) + p_n since each root satisfies x^2 = x + 1. So p_3 = 4, p_4 = 7, p_5 = 11, p_6 = 18.

q: Find the number of ordered pairs (x, y) of non-negative integers satisfying 2x + 3y = 120.
why: y must be even, y = 2k with k from 0 to 20, and then x = 60 - 3k is non-negative. This gives 21 pairs.

q: Real numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 5 and xy = 3. Find x^3 + y^3.
Let S = 1^2 - 2^2 + 3^2 - 4^2 + ... + 99^2 - 100^2. Find the remainder when |S| is divided by 100.
why: Pair the terms: (2k-1)^2 - (2k)^2 = -(4k-1). Adding for k = 1 to 50 gives -(1+2+...+100) = -5050. The absolute value 5050 leaves remainder 50.

q: A positive real number x satisfies x + 1/x = 3. Find x^4 + 1/x^4.
why: Squaring, x^2 + 1/x^2 = 9 - 2 = 7. Squaring again, x^4 + 1/x^4 = 49 - 2 = 47.

q: A function f on the non-negative integers satisfies f(0) = 5 and f(n+1) - f(n) = 4n + 1 for all n >= 0. Find f(6).
why: Summing the differences, f(n) = 5 + 2n(n-1) + n = 2n^2 - n + 5. Hence f(6) = 72 - 6 + 5 = 71.

q: How many three-digit numbers have their digits in strictly increasing order from left to right (for example 359)?
why: A valid number is determined by choosing 3 distinct digits from 1 to 9 (0 cannot appear, since it would have to come first), and writing them in the only increasing order. So the count is C(9,3).

q: In how many distinct ways can the letters of the word BANANA be arranged in a row so that no two letters A are next to each other?
why: Arrange B, N, N first: 3 distinct arrangements. This leaves 4 gaps (including the ends), and the three A's go into 3 different gaps: C(4,3)=4 ways. Total 3 x 4.

q: A club has 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can a committee of 3 members be chosen so that it has at least one boy and at least one girl?
why: Count all committees C(9,3)=84 and subtract the all-boy committees C(5,3)=10 and the all-girl committees C(4,3)=4. The result is 84-10-4.

q: What is the smallest positive integer n such that any n distinct integers chosen from 1, 2, ..., 50 must contain two integers whose difference is exactly 7?
why: Split 1..50 into 7 chains by remainder mod 7 (consecutive members of a chain differ by 7). Each chain has 7 or 8 terms, and from a chain of L terms at most ceil(L/2)=4 can be chosen with no two adjacent. So at most 7 x 4 = 28 numbers avoid the difference, and n = 29.

q: How many binary strings of length 8 (made of the digits 0 and 1) contain no two adjacent 1s?
why: Let a_n be the count. A string ends in 0 (preceded by any valid string of length n-1) or in 01 (preceded by a valid string of length n-2), so a_n = a_(n-1) + a_(n-2) with a_1=2, a_2=3. Continuing gives 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55.

q: Three fair six-sided dice, one red, one green and one blue, are rolled together. In how many of the 216 equally likely outcomes is the sum of the three numbers equal to 12?
why: Count solutions of r+g+b=12 with each variable from 1 to 6. Shift to x_i=r_i-1 in 0..5 with sum 9: C(11,2)=55 solutions, minus those with some x_i>=6 (3 x C(5,2)=30), giving 25.

q: For each of the 24 arrangements (a, b, c, d) of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, count the inversions, that is, pairs of positions i<j with the earlier entry larger than the later entry. What is the total of these counts over all 24 arrangements?
why: Each of the C(4,2)=6 pairs of positions is an inversion in exactly half of the arrangements (swapping the two entries reverses the pair). So the total is 6 x 24/2.

q: Six people sit around a round table, and two seatings that differ only by a rotation are regarded as the same. Three of the six are the friends A, B and C. In how many seatings are no two of A, B, C sitting next to each other?
why: Seat the other three people around the table first: (3-1)! = 2 ways. They create 3 gaps between neighbours, and A, B, C must go into different gaps, one per gap: 3! = 6 ways. Total 2 x 6.

q: How many ordered quadruples (x1, x2, x3, x4) of integers with 1 <= x_i <= 4 for every i satisfy x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 = 10?
why: Put y_i=x_i-1, so 0<=y_i<=3 and the sum is 6. Without the upper limit there are C(9,3)=84 solutions. Those with some y_i>=4 number 4 x C(5,3)=40 (two such variables would need a sum of at least 8). So 84-40.

q: Five different letters are put into five addressed envelopes, one letter in each envelope. In how many ways can this be done so that no letter is in its own envelope?
why: This is the number of derangements of 5 objects. Using D_n = (n-1)(D_(n-1)+D_(n-2)) with D_1=0, D_2=1: D_3=2, D_4=9, D_5=44.

q: In how many ways can 3 numbers be chosen from 1, 2, ..., 10 so that no two of the chosen numbers are consecutive integers?
why: Subtract 0, 1, 2 from the sorted chosen numbers a<b<c to get a, b-1, c-2, which are distinct numbers from 1 to 8. This is a bijection, so the answer is C(8,3).

q: A walker moves on lattice points from (0,0) to (4,4), each step being one unit right or one unit up. How many such routes avoid the point (2,2)?
why: All routes: C(8,4)=70. Routes through (2,2): C(4,2) x C(4,2)=36. So 70-36 = 34.

q: Two different numbers are chosen at random from 1, 2, ..., 20. The probability that their sum is even equals p/q in lowest terms. Find p + q.
why: The sum is even exactly when both numbers have the same parity: 2 x C(10,2)=90 favourable pairs out of C(20,2)=190. So the probability is 9/19 and p+q=28.

q: What is the largest number of integers that can be chosen from 1, 2, ..., 50 so that none of the chosen numbers is exactly twice another chosen number?
why: Group the numbers into chains m, 2m, 4m, ... starting from each odd m. Neighbours in a chain cannot both be chosen, so a chain with L terms gives at most ceil(L/2) numbers, and this is achievable. Adding ceil(L/2) over the 25 chains gives the maximum.

q: A string of length 10 has 3 letters X and 7 letters O. The X's form exactly two blocks of consecutive X's (for example OXXOOOXOOO has the blocks XX and X). How many such strings are there?
why: The blocks are XX and X, in either order. Treat the blocks as 2 objects placed among the 7 O's: choose 2 of the 8 gaps, C(8,2)=28, and the order of the blocks gives a factor 2, so 56.

q: Three married couples sit in a row of 6 chairs. In how many seatings does each husband sit immediately next to his own wife?
why: Treat each couple as a block: the 3 blocks can be ordered in 3! ways, and inside each block the two people can swap, giving 2^3. So 6 x 8.

q: How many four-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) with four different digits are multiples of 5? Give the remainder when the count is divided by 100.
why: If the last digit is 0, the first three digits are chosen in 9 x 8 x 7=504 ways. If it is 5, the first digit has 8 choices (not 0 or 5), the second 8, the third 7: 448. The total is 952, whose remainder modulo 100 is the answer.

q: How many strings of 6 letters, each letter A, B or C, have no two adjacent letters equal and also have the same first and last letter?
why: Let w_k be the number of such walks that start at a fixed letter and return to it after k steps (a string of k+1 letters). Then w_k = 2^(k-1) - w_(k-1), since all non-repeating continuations number 2^(k-1) and those ending elsewhere than the start must be removed. This gives w_5 = 10 for a fixed first letter. There are 3 choices for that letter, so 30.

q: A frog climbs a staircase of 8 steps, jumping up 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time (the last jump must land exactly on step 8). In how many different ways can it climb the staircase?
why: If s_n is the number of ways to reach step n, the last jump was 1, 2 or 3 steps, so s_n = s_(n-1)+s_(n-2)+s_(n-3), with s_0=1, s_1=1, s_2=2. Then s_3=4, s_4=7, s_5=13, s_6=24, s_7=44, s_8=81.

q: Three fair dice are rolled. The probability that the product of the three numbers is divisible by 4 equals p/q in lowest terms. Find p + q.
why: Use the complement. The product is not a multiple of 4 if all three numbers are odd (probability 1/8), or exactly one die shows an even number and it is 2 or 6 (3 x (1/3) x (1/2)^2 = 1/4). So the complement has probability 3/8 and the required probability is 5/8, giving p+q=13.

q: What is the smallest positive integer n such that any n distinct integers chosen from 1, 2, ..., 30 must contain two integers that differ by 4 or by 5?
why: Among 9 consecutive integers, arrange their positions on a cycle of length 9 in which two positions are joined when they differ by 4 or 5 (differences 4 and 5 correspond to the same cyclic distance 4 mod 9). An odd 9-cycle has no more than 4 pairwise non-adjacent points, so each block 1..9, 10..18, 19..27 holds at most 4 chosen numbers and 28, 29, 30 at most 3: at most 15 in all. Choosing the numbers with remainder 1, 2, 3, 4 mod 9, together with 28, 29, 30 and so on, achieves 15 so n = 16.

q: In how many ways can 3 different numbers be chosen from 1, 2, ..., 12 so that their sum is divisible by 3?
why: Each remainder class modulo 3 contains 4 numbers. The sum is a multiple of 3 if all three have the same remainder (3 x C(4,3)=12) or the remainders are 0, 1, 2, one each (4 x 4 x 4=64). Total 76.

q: In how many ways can 6 different people be split into 3 unordered groups, each group containing at least one person?
why: Count onto maps from 6 people to 3 labelled rooms by inclusion-exclusion: 3^6 - 3 x 2^6 + 3 = 540. Rooms are unlabelled, so divide by 3! = 6, giving 90.

q: A bag holds 3 red and 5 blue balls. Four balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that exactly 2 of the drawn balls are red equals p/q in lowest terms. Find p + q.
why: Favourable selections: C(3,2) x C(5,2)=30. All selections: C(8,4)=70. The probability is 30/70=3/7, so p+q=10.

q: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 13, BC = 14 and CA = 15. Let O be its circumcentre and let d be the distance from O to the side BC. Find 8d.
why: The circumradius is R = abc/(4K) = 13*14*15/(4*84) = 65/8. The perpendicular from O to BC bisects BC, so d^2 = R^2 - 7^2 = 1089/64, giving d = 33/8 and 8d = 33.

q: A convex quadrilateral in the coordinate plane has vertices (0,0), (9,2), (12,9) and (4,12). How many points with integer coordinates lie strictly inside it?
why: Use Pick's theorem: Area = I + B/2 - 1. The shoelace formula gives twice the area, and each side contributes gcd(|dx|,|dy|) lattice steps to the boundary count B. Solving for I gives the count of interior lattice points.

q: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle BAC = 100 degrees. The point D lies on side BC with BD = BA. Find angle DAC in degrees.
why: Angles B and C are 40 degrees each. Triangle ABD is isosceles with BA = BD and apex angle 40, so angle BAD = 70. Then angle DAC = 100 - 70 = 30.

q: x is an acute angle with sin x + cos x = 7/5. Find 125(sin^3 x + cos^3 x).
why: Squaring gives sin x cos x = 12/25. Then sin^3 x + cos^3 x = (sin x + cos x)(1 - sin x cos x) = (7/5)(13/25) = 91/125, so the required value is 91.

q: Two circles of radii 18 and 8 touch each other externally, and both touch a straight line l, lying on the same side of l. A third circle, in the gap bounded by the two circles and the line l, touches both circles and l. If its radius is r, find 25r.
why: Put l as the x-axis. The two big circles have centres 24 apart horizontally (since 24^2 + 10^2 = 26^2). For the small circle touching l at (x,0), tangency with each circle gives x^2 = 72r and (24 - x)^2 = 32r. Eliminating x yields r = 72/25, so 25r = 72.

q: In a circle of radius 25, two parallel chords of lengths 14 and 48 lie on the same side of the centre. Find the distance between them.
why: The distance of a chord of length L from the centre is sqrt(625 - (L/2)^2). That is 24 for the chord of length 14 and 7 for the chord of length 48. On the same side the gap is 24 - 7 = 17.

q: ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to CD, AB = 30 and CD = 20, and its area is 250. The diagonals meet at O. Find the area of triangle AOD.
why: Triangles AOB and COD are similar with ratio 3:2, so their areas are 9u and 4u. Triangles AOD and BOC each have area 6u (the geometric mean of 9u and 4u). The total 25u = 250 gives u = 10, so triangle AOD has area 60.

q: Points A(1,18) and B(16,6) are given. A point P moves along the line y = 2. Find the least possible value of PA + PB.
why: A and B lie on the same side of the line. Reflect B in y = 2 to get B'(16,-2). Then PA + PB = PA + PB' is least when P lies on segment AB', and this minimum is AB' = sqrt(15^2 + 20^2) = 25.

q: Find the value of cos^2(1 degree) + cos^2(2 degrees) + ... + cos^2(179 degrees).
why: Write cos^2 t = (1 + cos 2t)/2. The sum of cos(2k degrees) over k = 0..179 is 0 (equally spaced angles around a full circle), so over k = 1..179 it is -1. The total is (179 - 1)/2 = 89.

q: Find the value of tan 9 degrees - tan 27 degrees - tan 63 degrees + tan 81 degrees.
why: Since tan 81 = cot 9 and tan 63 = cot 27, the expression is (tan 9 + cot 9) - (tan 27 + cot 27) = 2/sin 18 - 2/sin 54. With sin 18 = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 and sin 54 = (sqrt5 + 1)/4 this equals 4.

q: Triangle ABC has sides 13, 14 and 15. Let O be its circumcentre and I its incentre. Find 64 * OI^2.
why: For this triangle the area is 84, so r = 4 and R = 65/8. Euler's relation gives OI^2 = R^2 - 2Rr = 4225/64 - 65 = 65/64, hence 64*OI^2 = 65.

q: In a right triangle the two legs have lengths 36 and 45. A circle whose centre lies on the hypotenuse touches both legs. Find its radius.
why: Put the right angle at the origin with legs on the axes. The centre is at (r,r) and lies on the hypotenuse x/45 + y/36 = 1, so r(1/45 + 1/36) = 1, giving r = 20.

q: In triangle ABC with area 210, the point D lies on BC with BD:DC = 2:3 and E lies on CA with CE:EA = 1:2. The lines AD and BE meet at P. Find the area of triangle ABP.
why: Use mass points (barycentric weights): D = (3B + 2C)/5 and E = (A + 2C)/3. The weights at A, B, C that satisfy both cevians are 1, 3, 2, so P has barycentric coordinates (1,3,2)/6. The area of ABP is 2/6 of 210 = 70.

q: From a point P a tangent PT of length 24 is drawn to a circle of radius 7. Find the least distance from P to a point of the circle.
why: The radius to T is perpendicular to PT, so PO = sqrt(24^2 + 7^2) = 25. The nearest point of the circle lies on PO, at distance 25 - 7 = 18.

q: In triangle ABC, angle B = 64 degrees and angle C = 38 degrees. O is the circumcentre and AD is the altitude from A, with D on BC. Find the angle OAD in degrees.
why: The angle between AO and the altitude AD is |B - C|: angle BAD = 90 - B = 26 and angle OAB = 90 - C = 52. Hence angle OAD = 52 - 26 = 26 degrees.

q: V0, V1, ..., V19 are the vertices, in order, of a regular 20-sided polygon inscribed in a circle. The chords V0V7 and V3V12 meet at a point inside the circle. Find the acute angle between them in degrees.
why: Each side of the polygon subtends 18 degrees at the centre. The angle between two intersecting chords is half the sum of the arcs cut off by the angle and its vertical opposite: here those arcs are V3V7 (4 steps) and V12V0 (8 steps). So the angle is (4 + 8)*18/2 = 108 degrees, and its acute supplement is 72 degrees.

q: A circle passes through the points (0,0), (12,0) and (3,9). Its area is k*pi. Find k.
why: The centre lies on the perpendicular bisector x = 6 of the chord from (0,0) to (12,0). Equating distances to (0,0) and (3,9) gives the centre (6,3). Then R^2 = 36 + 9 = 45, so k = 45.

q: The midpoints of the sides of a regular hexagon of area 96 are joined in order to form a smaller hexagon. Find the area of the smaller hexagon.
why: The new hexagon is regular and its side is the distance between midpoints of adjacent sides, which is (sqrt3/2) times the original side. The area scales by (sqrt3/2)^2 = 3/4, so the area is 96*3/4 = 72.

q: P is a point inside a rectangle ABCD (vertices in order) with PA = 9, PB = 5 and PC = 13. Find PD.
why: For any point in a rectangle, PA^2 + PC^2 = PB^2 + PD^2 (drop perpendiculars to the sides). So PD^2 = 81 + 169 - 25 = 225 and PD = 15.

q: How many angles x with 0 <= x < 360 (in degrees) satisfy sin x + sin 3x + sin 5x + sin 7x = 0?
why: Pair the terms: sin x + sin 7x = 2 sin 4x cos 3x and sin 3x + sin 5x = 2 sin 4x cos x, so the sum is 4 sin 4x cos 2x cos x. The zeros of sin 4x are the multiples of 45 degrees (8 values), and the zeros of cos 2x and cos x are already among them, so there are 8 solutions.

q: Find the value of tan^2(pi/7) + tan^2(2pi/7) + tan^2(3pi/7).
why: From tan 7x = 0 with x = k pi/7 the numbers t = tan(k pi/7) satisfy t^6 - 21t^4 + 35t^2 - 7 = 0 (for k = 1..6). The three values u = t^2 are therefore the roots of u^3 - 21u^2 + 35u - 7 = 0, and by Vieta their sum is 21.

q: ABCD is a square of side 30 with vertices A, B, C, D in order. M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of BC. The lines DM and AN meet at P. Find the sum of the distances from P to the sides AB and AD.
why: Place A at the origin, B = (30,0), D = (0,30). Line DM is x/15 + y/30 = 1 and line AN is y = x/2. Solving gives P = (12,6), so the distances to AD and AB are 12 and 6, total 18.

q: In a triangle two sides have lengths 5 and 8 and the angle between them is 60 degrees. If R is the circumradius of the triangle, find 3R^2.
why: By the cosine rule the third side satisfies x^2 = 25 + 64 - 40 = 49, so x = 7. The sine rule gives 2R = 7/sin 60 = 14/sqrt3, so R^2 = 49/3 and 3R^2 = 49.

q: Find the number of points (x,y) with integer coordinates that lie on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1625.
why: Since 1625 = 5^3 * 13 with both primes of the form 4k+1, the number of integer solutions of x^2 + y^2 = n is 4 times the number of divisors of n, namely 4*(3+1)*(1+1) = 32.

q: From an external point P two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle with centre O, and angle APB = 40 degrees. A third tangent touches the circle at a point C on the minor arc AB (the arc nearer to P) and meets the lines PA and PB at Q and R. Find angle QOR in degrees.
why: The circle is the excircle of triangle PQR opposite P, so O is the excentre. The excentre angle satisfies angle QOR = 90 - (angle P)/2 = 90 - 20 = 70 degrees.

q: Find the remainder when 7^2026 is divided by 100.
why: Since 7^2 = 49 and 7^4 = 2401, we have 7^4 = 1 (mod 100). As 2026 = 4*506 + 2, the power reduces to 7^2 = 49.

q: How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 200 satisfy gcd(n, 36) = 1?
why: gcd(n,36) = 1 means n is divisible by neither 2 nor 3, i.e. n leaves remainder 1 or 5 on division by 6. Each block of 6 consecutive integers has 2 such numbers, and 200 = 6*33 + 2 gives 66 from the full blocks. The leftover numbers 199 and 200 are 1 and 2 mod 6, so 199 adds one more: 67.

q: Find the smallest positive integer that is divisible by 6 and has exactly 12 positive divisors.
why: Check multiples of 6 in order and count divisors from the prime factorisation. The numbers 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 have 4, 6, 6, 8, 8, 9, 8, 10, 8 divisors, and 60 = 2^2*3*5 has (2+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 12.

q: Find the sum of the digits of the smallest positive multiple of 45 all of whose digits are 0 or 7.
why: A multiple of 45 is a multiple of 5 and of 9. Ending in 0 handles divisibility by 5. Divisibility by 9 needs the digit sum, which is 7 times the number of 7s, to be a multiple of 9, so there are at least nine 7s. The smallest number is 7777777770, with digit sum 63.

q: The number 2026 is written in base 7. Find the sum of its digits in that representation.
why: Divide repeatedly by 7: 2026 = 5*343 + 311, 311 = 6*49 + 17, and 17 = 2*7 + 3. So 2026 is 5623 in base 7, and the digit sum is 5 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 16.

q: How many ordered pairs (a, b) of positive integers have gcd(a, b) = 6 and lcm(a, b) = 360?
why: Write a = 6m and b = 6n with gcd(m, n) = 1. Then lcm(a, b) = 6mn = 360, so mn = 60 = 2^2 * 3 * 5. Each of the three prime powers goes wholly to m or wholly to n, giving 2^3 = 8 ordered pairs.

q: How many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfy 7x + 11y = 500?
why: Reducing modulo 7 gives 4y = 3 (mod 7), so y = 6 (mod 7). The values y = 6, 13, 20, 27, 34, 41 give positive integers x = (500 - 11y)/7, and larger y makes x non-positive. That is 6 pairs.

q: Find the largest prime factor of 2^20 - 1.
why: Factor with differences of squares: 2^20 - 1 = (2^10 - 1)(2^10 + 1) = 1023 * 1025 = (3*11*31) * (5^2 * 41). The largest prime factor is 41.

q: When 100! is written in base 12, how many zeros does it end with?
why: The number of trailing zeros in base 12 is the largest k with 12^k = 2^(2k) * 3^k dividing 100!. The exponent of 2 in 100! is 97 and that of 3 is 48, so k = min(floor(97/2), 48) = 48.

q: Find the smallest positive integer n that leaves remainder 2 on division by 3, remainder 3 on division by 5 and remainder 4 on division by 7.
why: List the numbers that are 4 mod 7: 4, 11, 18, 25, 32, 39, 46, 53. Test the other two conditions on each; 53 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3 and remainder 3 on division by 5, and no earlier one does.

q: Let S be the sum of all positive divisors of 360. Find the remainder when S is divided by 100.
why: Since 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5, the divisor sum is (1+2+4+8)(1+3+9)(1+5) = 15 * 13 * 6 = 1170. The remainder on dividing by 100 is 70.

q: How many primes p less than 100 are there such that 2p + 1 is also prime?
why: Test each prime below 100 and check whether 2p + 1 is prime. The primes p = 2, 3, 5, 11, 23, 29, 41, 53, 83, 89 work, and the rest fail, so the count is 10.

q: Find the last two digits of 13^169, as a number from 0 to 99.
How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 100 satisfy n^2 = 1 (mod 24)?
why: If n is coprime to 6, then n^2 = 1 (mod 8) and n^2 = 1 (mod 3), hence n^2 = 1 (mod 24). Conversely, n^2 = 1 (mod 24) forces n to be odd and not a multiple of 3. So count n <= 100 coprime to 6: 100 - 50 - 33 + 16 = 33.

q: The digits of a positive integer multiply to 720. Find the sum of the digits of the smallest such integer.
why: Three digits cannot multiply to 720 because the largest product of three digits is 729 but 720 = 2^4*3^2*5 has no split into three digits at most 9 (it would need 8*9*10). So at least four digits are needed. To make the number smallest, take the smallest possible leading digit: 2 * 5 * 8 * 9 = 720 gives 2589, and a leading 1 is impossible. The digit sum is 24.

q: Find the sum of all positive integers n for which n + 3 divides n^2 + 27.
why: Since n = -3 (mod n+3), n^2 + 27 = 9 + 27 = 36 (mod n+3). So n + 3 divides 36 with n + 3 > 3, giving n + 3 in {4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36} and n in {1, 3, 6, 9, 15, 33}. Their sum is 67.

q: How many positive divisors of 12! are perfect squares?
why: 12! = 2^10 * 3^5 * 5^2 * 7 * 11. A divisor is a square exactly when every exponent is even: the exponent of 2 has 6 choices (0, 2, ..., 10), of 3 has 3 choices, of 5 has 2 choices, and 7 and 11 only 1 choice each. The total is 6 * 3 * 2 = 36.

q: Find the sum of the digits of 3333333^2.
why: Square the number directly: 3333333^2 = 11111108888889. Adding its digits (six 1s... in fact seven 1s... checked by the pattern 1111110 8888889) gives the sum.

q: How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 150 are divisible by exactly one of 3 and 5 (that is, by 3 or 5 but not by both)?
why: There are 50 multiples of 3, 30 multiples of 5 and 10 multiples of 15 up to 150. Remove the common multiples from each list: (50 - 10) + (30 - 10) = 60.

q: Find the exponent of the highest power of 7 that divides 200!.
why: By Legendre's formula the exponent is floor(200/7) + floor(200/49) + floor(200/343) = 28 + 4 + 0 = 32.

q: How many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfy 1/x + 1/y = 1/12?
why: Clearing denominators gives xy = 12x + 12y, i.e. (x - 12)(y - 12) = 144, and both factors must be positive. The pairs therefore correspond to the positive divisors of 144 = 2^4 * 3^2, which number (4+1)(2+1) = 15.

q: Find the smallest positive integer k such that 2^k - 1 is divisible by 77.
why: We need 2^k = 1 modulo 7 and modulo 11. The order of 2 modulo 7 is 3 and modulo 11 is 10, so k must be a multiple of both, and the least such k is lcm(3, 10) = 30.

q: How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 100 make n^2 + n + 1 divisible by 7?
why: Checking n = 0, 1, ..., 6 modulo 7 shows that n^2 + n + 1 is divisible by 7 only for n = 2 and n = 4. Among 1..100 there are 15 numbers that are 2 (mod 7) (2, 9, ..., 100) and 14 that are 4 (mod 7) (4, 11, ..., 95), for a total of 29.

q: Let n be the largest positive integer such that n + 7 divides n^3 + 1000. Find the remainder when n is divided by 100.
why: Since n = -7 (mod n+7), n^3 + 1000 = -343 + 1000 = 657 (mod n+7). So n + 7 divides 657 = 9 * 73, and the largest choice n + 7 = 657 gives n = 650, whose remainder on division by 100 is 50.

q: How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 210 satisfy n^2 = n (mod 210)?
why: Since 210 = 2 * 3 * 5 * 7, the condition n(n - 1) = 0 modulo 210 means that modulo each of these primes n is 0 or 1 (as a prime dividing a product of consecutive integers divides one of them). By the Chinese remainder theorem that gives 2^4 = 16 residues, each represented once in 1..210.

q: Two point charges, +4q and -q, are held a distance d apart in vacuum. On the line through them there is exactly one finite point where the net electric field is zero. Where is it?
why: Between the charges both fields point the same way, so zero field needs a point outside, nearer the smaller charge. With x measured from -q on the far side: 4q/(d+x)^2 = q/x^2, so 2x = d + x and x = d. A point between the charges fails because the two fields add there.
opts: At distance d/2 from -q, between the charges
At distance d/3 from -q, between the charges
At distance d from -q, on the side away from +4q
At distance 2d from -q, on the side away from +4q

q: A 2 uF parallel-plate capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric slab of constant 4 is slid in to fill the gap completely. By how much does the stored energy decrease?
why: Initial energy = (1/2)(2x10^-6)(100)^2 = 10 mJ. With the charge fixed, C becomes 4 times larger and U = Q^2/2C falls to 2.5 mJ, a decrease of 7.5 mJ. 2.5 mJ is the final energy, not the decrease, and 30 mJ would be the increase if the battery stayed connected.

q: A 3 uF and a 6 uF capacitor are joined in series across a 90 V supply. What is the potential difference across the 3 uF capacitor?
why: In series both carry the same charge: Q = (3 x 6/9) uF x 90 V = 180 uC. Then V across the 3 uF capacitor = Q/C = 180/3 = 60 V. The smaller capacitor takes the larger share; 30 V is the share of the 6 uF capacitor.

q: A point charge +2Q sits at the centre of a thick conducting spherical shell whose net charge is +Q. What is the charge on the outer surface of the shell?
why: The inner surface acquires -2Q to cancel the field inside the conductor. The shell's net charge is +Q, so the outer surface carries Q - (-2Q) = +3Q. Answering +Q forgets that the induced charge on the inner surface must be balanced by extra charge on the outer one.

q: Three point charges q, 2q and -3q are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. What is the electrostatic potential energy of the system? (k = 1/(4 pi epsilon_0))
why: Add the three pair energies: k[(q)(2q) + (q)(-3q) + (2q)(-3q)]/a = k q^2(2 - 3 - 6)/a = -7kq^2/a. Dropping one pair gives the tempting -1 or -9, and the sign is negative because the opposite-sign pairs dominate.

q: An electric dipole of moment 4x10^-9 C m lies along a uniform field of 5x10^3 N/C. How much work must an external agent do to turn it slowly through 120 degrees?
why: Work = pE(cos 0 - cos 120) = pE(1 + 0.5) = 1.5 pE. Here pE = 4x10^-9 x 5x10^3 = 2x10^-5 J, so W = 3.0x10^-5 J. 2.0x10^-5 J is the work for 90 degrees and 4.0x10^-5 J for 180 degrees; 1.0x10^-5 J uses only cos 120.

q: A wire of resistance 4 ohm is uniformly stretched to three times its length, then cut into three equal pieces, which are connected in parallel. What is the resistance of the combination?
why: Stretching to 3 times the length at constant volume multiplies R by 9, giving 36 ohm. Each of the three pieces is 12 ohm, and three in parallel give 4 ohm. If you forget the area shrinks, you get pieces of 4 ohm and 4/3 ohm, which is wrong.

q: A potentiometer wire is 2.0 m long and has resistance 10 ohm. It is connected in series with a 30 ohm resistor and a 4.0 V driver cell of negligible internal resistance. A cell of unknown emf balances at 140 cm along the wire. What is the emf of this cell?
why: Current = 4/(10+30) = 0.1 A, so the voltage across the wire is 1.0 V over 2.0 m, a gradient of 0.5 V/m. The emf is 0.5 x 1.40 = 0.70 V. Using the full 4 V over the wire (ignoring the series resistor) gives the tempting 2.80 V.

q: A 12 V cell of internal resistance 1 ohm and a 6 V cell of internal resistance 2 ohm are connected in parallel, positive to positive, and then across an external 4 ohm resistor. What current flows in the 4 ohm resistor?
why: Equivalent emf = (12/1 + 6/2)/(1 + 1/2) = 10 V and equivalent internal resistance = 2/3 ohm. Current = 10/(4 + 2/3) = 2.14 A. Treating the cells as being in series (18/7 = 2.57 A) or ignoring the second cell (12/4 = 3 A) is wrong.

q: A 100 W and a 60 W bulb, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Assuming the resistances stay constant, what power does the 100 W bulb dissipate?
why: R = V^2/P gives 484 ohm for the 100 W bulb and 807 ohm for the 60 W bulb. The current is 220/1291 = 0.170 A, so P = I^2R = 14.1 W for the 100 W bulb. The 38 W figure is the total power of the series pair, and 23 W is the 60 W bulb: in series the larger resistance gets more power.

q: A copper wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries a steady current of 2.0 A. Free electron density in copper is 8.5x10^28 per m^3 and e = 1.6x10^-19 C. What is the drift speed of the electrons?
why: A = pi(0.5x10^-3)^2 = 7.85x10^-7 m^2, so v = I/(neA) = 2/(8.5x10^28 x 1.6x10^-19 x 7.85x10^-7) = 1.9x10^-4 m/s. Using the diameter as the radius gives 4.7x10^-5 m/s, and taking A = d^2 gives 1.5x10^-4 m/s.

q: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4 times, charge 2 times that of the proton) enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it with the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of the radii of their circular paths, r(proton) : r(alpha)?
why: From r = sqrt(2mK)/(qB), r is proportional to sqrt(m)/q. For the proton this is sqrt(m)/q; for the alpha it is sqrt(4m)/(2q) = sqrt(m)/q. The ratio is 1 : 1. The 1 : sqrt(2) answer belongs to equal accelerating potential, not equal kinetic energy.

q: Two long straight parallel wires 20 cm apart carry currents of 3 A and 9 A in opposite directions. The net magnetic field is zero at exactly one point on the line through them. How far is that point from the 3 A wire?
why: Between opposite currents the fields add, so the null point lies outside, on the side of the smaller current. Setting 3/x = 9/(x + 20) gives 3x + 60 = 9x, so x = 10 cm. Taking the point between the wires (5 cm) is wrong because the fields would reinforce there.

q: A long wire carrying 5.0 A runs along a straight line through a point O, follows a semicircular arc of radius 10 cm centred on O, and then continues straight along the same line. What is the magnetic field at O? (mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A)
why: The straight parts pass through O along their own length and give no field there. A semicircle gives half the field of a full loop: B = mu_0 I/(4R) = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 5/(0.4) = 1.6x10^-5 T. The full-loop value 3.1x10^-5 T is the tempting wrong answer.

q: A rectangular coil of 50 turns and area 0.020 m^2 carries 2.0 A in a uniform field of 0.50 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 30 degrees with the field direction. What is the torque on the coil?
why: Torque = NIAB sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the coil's normal and the field. Here theta = 60 degrees, not 30. NIAB = 50 x 2 x 0.02 x 0.5 = 1.0 N m, so the torque = 1.0 x sin 60 = 0.87 N m. Using 30 degrees gives 0.50 N m and the maximum value is 1.00 N m.

q: A metal rod 0.50 m long slides at a steady 4.0 m/s on two horizontal frictionless rails joined by a 2.0 ohm resistor, in a uniform vertical field of 0.20 T. The rails and rod have negligible resistance. What power must be supplied to keep the rod moving at constant speed?
why: emf = Blv = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4 V, so I = 0.2 A and the retarding force is BIl = 0.02 N. Power = Fv = 0.02 x 4 = 0.080 W, which equals emf^2/R. The 0.16 W figure comes from forgetting to divide by R, and 0.020 W is the force in newtons.

q: A circular loop of radius 10 cm and resistance 2.0 ohm has its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.50 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.10 s. What total charge flows through the loop?
why: Charge = change in flux/R = (0.5 x pi x 0.01)/2 = 7.85x10^-3 C, independent of the time taken. Dividing by the time as well, or forgetting a factor of 2 in the resistance step, gives the other values.

q: A coil of inductance 2.0 H and resistance 10 ohm is connected suddenly to a 20 V battery of negligible internal resistance. What is the current in the circuit 0.20 s later? (e = 2.718)
why: The time constant is L/R = 0.20 s, so at t = 0.20 s the current is (V/R)(1 - e^-1) = 2.0 x 0.632 = 1.26 A. The final value is 2.0 A, and 0.74 A is 2/e, the amount still missing from the final value rather than the current itself.

q: A current i = 3 + 4 sin(wt) amperes flows through a resistor. What is the rms value of this current?
why: Mean square = (steady part)^2 + (rms of sine)^2 = 9 + 16/2 = 17, so I_rms = sqrt(17) = 4.1 A. Adding the rms values directly (3 + 4/sqrt(2) = 5.8 A) or adding the squares of the peaks (5.0 A) is the tempting mistake.

q: A series circuit has R = 20 ohm, L = 0.10 H and C = 10 uF, and is driven by a 100 V (rms) source whose frequency is varied to resonance. What is the rms voltage across the inductor at resonance?
why: Resonance angular frequency = 1/sqrt(LC) = 1000 rad/s, so X_L = wL = 100 ohm. The current is V/R = 5 A, so V_L = I X_L = 500 V. 100 V is the source voltage, which would be correct only if R were as big as X_L.

q: A series circuit has R = 30 ohm, inductive reactance 70 ohm and capacitive reactance 30 ohm, connected to a 100 V (rms) supply. What is the average power dissipated?
why: Net reactance = 70 - 30 = 40 ohm, so Z = 50 ohm and I = 2 A. Average power = I^2R = 4 x 30 = 120 W. 200 W is V x I with power factor ignored, and 333 W is V^2/R with the reactance ignored.

q: A step-down transformer converts 2200 V to 220 V and has an efficiency of 90 per cent. It delivers 11 kW to a load. What current does it draw from the 2200 V supply?
